367.t: Gerald joins Basie to replace Snooky
367.s: Gerald was called to replace Snooky in Basie's band, went to Chicago, Snooky never returned, and Basie needed a writer.
367.q: Yeah. Isn’t that funny? Who do you think, when I joined Count Basie, who do you think I was supposed to replace? Snooky Young. Snooky left the band. They were playing someplace, and Basie called me and he says, “Snooky there had to go back East, Gerald,” and I played a couple of days with him at…

367.t: Snooky returns to Dayton for ten years, then rejoins Basie
367.s: Snooky foresaw the decline and went home to Dayton for ten years, then returned to Basie's comeback band, whose sections he lists.
367.q: I foreseen it coming, that’s why I split. Really. That’s the truth. I seen it coming in California and I split. They didn’t know where I was. But I had gone home. I mean, I’m a youngster and I didn’t pay it no attention, I said, well I’m going home you know. I packed my things.

367.t: What Basie was like to work for
367.s: Basie was easygoing, gambled and was loved by the sporting crowd; Snooky recalls a command performance for the Queen in 1959.
367.q: All you had to do for Basie is play. Play. Because he would kind of let you mess up a little bit, but not too much. He didn’t want to be, you know what I mean, like catch some guys overdoing it and drinking and whatnot. But he’ll let you go on and do that ‘cause he like the taste himself a little…

367.t: A month with Basie replacing Buck Clayton
367.s: When Basie came through Dayton, Young went on the road for about a month filling in for Buck Clayton.
367.q: Let me think, let me see now. Yes, I was in there in ‘42. Oh, I think…yes, that‘s when they came through and I, and I think they needed a trumpet player because…what‘s his name? Buck Clayton…

367.t: Meeting Thad Jones and the Basie trumpet section
367.s: Young first met Thad Jones in Detroit; the Basie section was Thad, Joe Newman, Wendell Culley and Young.
367.q: No, that wasn‘t the first time I met him, the first time I met Thad was in Detroit when I had my band. That‘s before it went back in and before he went with Basie, before he got with Basie, because Basie, we was in Basie‘s, the new band he had put together. Thad and Gerald…Thad…Joe Newman…Wendell…

367.t: Wendell Culley walks off after Marshal Royal hollers
367.s: Marshal Royal shouted at Wendell Culley, who nodded out on stage, and Culley packed his horn and was never seen again.
367.q: Yeah. Wendell Culley got off the bandstand and walked off. Wendell Culley was a sweetheart, man. You talking about a nice man and he could play. He played just like he was, he even wanted to play Li’l Darlin’. He was just so, I don‘t see how anybody could turn around and holler at him.; Marshal…

367.t: Basie as a bandleader, and leaving to join Gerald Wilson's band
367.s: Young calls Basie a good boss who let a manager run things; he once left for Gerald Wilson's band, which broke up in St. Louis, and Basie took him back.
367.q: Oh, Count Basie, he was a nice bandleader, man. He was, well…that‘s a good question. Count Basie was a nice cat and he was, he always had a manager or something with him that used to kind of run things. But Count Basie used to be in the know of what‘s going on, too, but he would let this other guy…

367.t: Replacing Buck Clayton, then playing lead in Basie's trumpet section
367.s: Young explains the first stint was a month for Buck Clayton and the later one as first trumpet, with Sweets taking the solos.
367.q: When I first went in there, I went in there and replaced…

367.t: The happy Basie trumpet section of Thad, Joe Newman and Albert Aarons
367.s: Young lists the later Basie four-trumpet section and says a section that likes each other plays well.
367.q: Yeah, Count Basie…the five trumpets was Thad Jones, me, Wendell Cully passed so they got…who did they get in place of him? They didn‘t have five trumpets.

367.t: Personnel on The Atomic Basie and a band with no enemies
367.s: Brown reads the 1957 Atomic Basie lineup and Young recalls a friendly band where Basie would call out a flat first half and then the band would light up.
367.q: That was a good band, man. You‘re talking about a, that band was, it was really, was he, it was a funny thing, that band they like one another. Everybody liked, there was no enemies in that band. And that band, it‘s a funny thing, they just, sometimes the band would play and Basie we‘d play the…

367.t: Clayton-Hamilton band compared with the Basie band
367.s: Young says his current Clayton-Hamilton band has the same spark as the 1957 Basie band.
367.q: That‘s what I‘m talking about. This band, when it fires up, you feel the same spark in this band that happened in that band. That‘s true.

367.t: Never wanting to be a leader; Frank Foster and Basie's later leaders
367.s: Young says he never wanted to lead, as with Sweets and Frank Wess, and talks about helping Frank Foster and who led the Basie band afterwards.
367.q: Like, like Quincy or some of the guys I played with that played music and went on to become band leaders, like Gerald Wilson even. He was a side man and went on to be, he turned out to be a big, big, big man, as a leader, you know. But I never had that in my mind, I never wanted to be a leader. I…

367.t: Sonny Cohn and Al Aarons join the trumpet section
367.s: Young recalls Sonny Cohn replacing Wendell Culley, who walked off after Marshal Royal's outburst, and Al Aarons arriving.
367.q: Sonny Cohn. Well, I remember when Sonny Cohn came to the band and I remember when Al Aarons come to the band. Who did Sonny Cohn? Oh, that‘s when the trumpet player that, what‘s his name said something to and he got off and left.

367.t: Praise for Sonny Payne and the Basie band
367.s: Young and Brown agree Sonny Payne was phenomenal and Young says he loved Basie's band.
367.q: He was phenomenal, man. You know what I‘m saying. Yeah, he‘d do everything. And, it would come out!

367.t: Replacing Ed Lewis as Basie's first trumpet
367.s: Young says he replaced Ed Lewis, whose age probably ended his time, and that doing so helped put swing into the band.
367.q: I replaced Ed Lewis. I replaced Ed Lewis and the only way I replaced Ed Lewis, I think his age got him out of Count Basie‘s band. And Ed Lewis was a hell of a first trumpet player, but I worked beside him for a long time when we played in Basie‘s band and Ed Lewis was still in there, but I guess,…

367.s: Brown mentions a 1962 Stockholm video of Basie with Young and plans to show footage later.
367.q: I think, yeah, I was with Basie then.

367.t: Rejoining Basie from 1945 and the dates to the Tonight Show
367.s: Brown and Young sort out whether he was with Basie 1945-48 and that he stayed until joining the Tonight Show in 1962.
367.q: Yes, that‘s right, and I stayed in Count Basie‘s band until I went on the Tonight

101.t: Basie's light and comic book in Wilkes-Barre
101.s: Terry's favorite Basie story: sharing a landlady's room, Basie's reading light and 'put it back'.
101.q: Yeah, between those two beautiful people, we could write books and talk for ages. I have to tell you my favorite Basie story, and I’ve told this many times, but when we were with the small group after he broke up the big band —

101.t: Basie stops the bus on John Williams
101.s: Williams relays how Basie let John Williams go over an overheard insult and how he handled grumbling musicians.
101.q: You couldn’t pull no wool on him. He knew everything.

101.t: Basie follows Terry home for ham and cabbage
101.s: Basie rode home with Terry from Birdland and ended up eating ham and cabbage at his apartment.
101.q: At the same time. So we’re in the Band Box with Charlie Parker, Duke Ellington and downstairs is Basie. You might have been down there with him. But anyhow, I used to snitch a ride home every night with Catherine, Basie’s wife used to pick him up and they had to pass by my house. So I’d ride home.…

101.t: Dinner at Earl Hines's house; Basie ate dessert first
101.s: The Basie band was fed at Earl Hines's Philadelphia home, with Basie eating his dessert first.

101.t: Canada border narcotics trouble and Basie's advice
101.s: Two band members were barred from Canada; subs were found and Basie advised just getting a piano player and going on.
101.q: One and one is eleven. I can figure that out.

101.t: Basie's house on the Bahamas golf course
101.s: They discuss how Basie came to buy a Bahamas house on a golf course, after Catherine's real estate junket.
101.q: Well I thought he got the idea, he came, Catherine came down on a real estate junket and I had bought a lot down there. So they were showing them around, right across from Stone Crab. So they were showing them around and they said, “this lot over here, you probably wouldn’t know him but it belongs…

101.t: Auditioning for Basie with Hey Rube
101.s: Terry plays the high lead part, hitting an A, and gets the Basie job.
101.q: I’m trying to think where I was. Yeah, I was in New York with – it might have been the Barnet band or either George Hudson’s band, and I made an audition with Basie’s band at Nola Studio. They passed out some music with some very difficult parts to it, some lead trumpet parts that Sweets – Harry…

101.t: The spirit and personnel of Basie's Old Testament band
101.s: Basie's down-to-earth leadership and the trumpet, trombone and sax sections.
101.q: The spirit of the band was great, because Basie – it all stems from Basie. He himself was a real down-to-earth cat. He was one of the boys, one of the gang. He always like to hang out with the cats. The spirit of everybody therein was more or less like Basie’s. He was a real groovy cat. Whatever…

101.t: The Basie audition: Hey Rube and the high A
101.s: Retelling the Nola's Studio audition, the high C's of Hey Rube and the A on South.
101.q: I was in New York, and the Basie band was in the market for a trumpet player. So they hired me to come in to rehearse with the band at Nola’s Studio. Nola’s Studio at that time was at 1619 Broadway, up in the penthouse. So we went up. It was customary – on the whole scene, it was customary to give…

101.t: Basie's debt and the small group at the Brass Rail
101.s: Basie cut the band to a septet to pay off debts to the office; Terry recruits Bob Graf; DeFranco paid more than Basie.
101.q: It was due basically to Basie’s indebtedness to the office. He owed the office a lot of money, and he got in trouble through the medium of the horses. He was a big horse player. I guess that’s where Al Grey got his training from. But Basie, every time he’s got $10 in his hand, [Terry whistles],…

101.t: Wardell Gray and Bob Graf in the septet
101.s: Terry was best man at Wardell Gray's wedding; Graf is scouted away by Woody Herman; Terry's estimate of Gray.
101.q: Absolutely. I was the best man at his wedding while he was in that group. He had been married to Geri Gray, the dancer who just recently passed away. That’s how Geri Gray got her name, from Wardell Gray. At this point he was married to Dorothy. He was getting married to Dorothy. They got married in…

101.t: Burning the band uniforms in Toronto
101.s: Terry and Marshal Royal set fire to their old uniforms outside Basie's door; Al Killian's death is recalled.
101.q: That is a fact. We were in Toronto at a club – I can’t think of the name of the club. We had been wearing these old ragged uniforms for years. [They] were actually torn all up on the sleeves. The liner was ripped out. It was really horrible. We said, “Basie, why don’t we go get some” – “Aw, don’t…

101.t: The New Testament band was a letdown
101.s: Terry says the post-septet band had players not suited to the Basie style.
101.q: It was horrible, because he had people in there who were not traditionalized. At least they didn’t – they weren’t really ready for that type of life, the laid-back, relaxed indulgence in playing. A lot of them were – come from different areas, different walks of life, and they had different…

101.t: Other musicians Terry recruited for Basie and Ellington
101.s: Bernie Peacock, the Wilkins brothers and Paul Campbell; both leaders trusted his recommendations.
101.q: Yeah, I got a lot of people in the band from time to time: Bernie Peacock, Ernie, Jimmy. [Let’s] see. Who else? I got Paul Campbell.

101.t: Conducting for Basie and being vetoed as his successor
101.s: Terry sometimes led the band; Norman Granz blocked his taking over after Basie died.
101.q: He would have a lot of us from time to time do – kick the band off and stop it or something like that, but if he was going to be off the stand or something, socializing heavily or something, we – either one of us would take the responsibility of doing that, but for the most part, he would get a…

101.t: Williams's first Basie job in Norfolk
101.s: On the first job after Williams joined, Basie opened with 'What Am I Here For' at a Navy officers' dance.

86.t: Taking solos, Prez's bell, and how he became 'Sweets'
86.s: Prez rang a bell to fire poor soloists; Edison got his nickname after a muted solo, and a trumpeter named Frank Beard was fired over a solo.
86.ch: Joining Basie and life on the bus
86.q: I just got up and took me a solo. I just gorilla’d me a solo. They had no music so what the hell, I’d just go take me a solo. And if he was playing, Basie would never object to you taking as long as you would be playing something because I remember a couple of trombone players came in the band and…

86.t: Basie's piano playing and his place among his men
86.s: He says Basie could stride, recalls a Pablo date with Basie, and tells of Basie riding the bus and enduring humiliations.
86.ch: Leading the Basie band: music, rivals and recordings
86.q: No, not necessarily. Because when I first joined the band he was playing. Basie was a good piano player. People nowadays think he couldn’t play, this generation, Basie could play. He’s got some records out, he could stride.

86.t: Why Basie cut his men loose
86.s: Edison believes Basie meant to free the veterans to lead their own groups.
86.ch: After Basie: freelancing, JATP and Hollywood
86.q: A lot of the guys resented it but I looked at it like I gave him all the…there was no doubt in my mind that he did that for a reason. Because all of us achieved more by what he did than we would have by staying with his band. I always thought that he thought, “Well, these guys have done enough with…

86.t: The thrill of Basie's band and Basie as leader
86.s: Edison calls the Basie band the greatest thrill of his life and praises Basie's humor and respect for soloists.
86.q: And, gee whiz, what a thrill it was to play with that band. That was the greatest thrill of my life, being a member of Count Basie's aggregation.

86.t: Years with Basie, 1938 to 1950 and after
86.s: Edison was with Basie from 1938 to 1950 and returned later, treating the band as his chair.
86.q: From '38 to '50. Then I went back, you know. And I still go back. So I've been with Basie over a period of 25 years or 30 years. Although I leave and -- but, you know, I still consider that as my chair, you know. And I'm quite sure that anybody who has ever been in his band that is still active,…

86.t: Why Basie took over the Moten band
86.s: Edison says Basie was popular and, as a pianist, the logical leader, as pianists often led bands then.
86.q: I don't know how he inherited the band but I think he was just a very popular guy, you know. And some guys around there that he knew, like Piney Brown and all those guys, they gave him the name of "Count", you know.

86.t: Solos credited to Buck Clayton that were really his
86.s: Edison names solos he took on Basie records, such as Every Tub, Sent for You Yesterday and Easy Does It, and Dance offers to correct the listings.
86.q: Well, yeah, that was me. I took a lot of solos, you know, that Buck got the credit for. Like "Every Tub", "Sent for You Yesterday."

86.t: Basie's small group and its reception
86.s: Basie formed a small group, kept only Clark Terry, and drew static from audiences.
86.ch: After Basie: freelancing, JATP and Hollywood
86.q: Buddy DeFranco and Serge Chaloff. Well, Gus Johnson had been in the band before, in the old Basie band in Kansas City. But he had a bunch of guys that weren’t affiliated with Count Basie so far as the public was concerned at all. And he did get a lot of static at places that he played. Not that the…

86.t: Why Basie's small band left him out
86.s: Edison felt lost and still doesn't know why Basie did not take him.
86.q: I don't know. I don't know. That's what everybody wonders today, you know, why didn't he take myself? And -- like with Dicky Wells, the older guys out of the band. That's Basie's -- and Serge Chaloff and Buddy DeFranco. I couldn't see why he took any of them because Basie had enough soloists in his…

86.t: Learning Basie had gone to Chicago without him
86.s: He, Freddie Green and Ted Donnelly heard the news outside the Hotel Theresa, and he realized how dependent he had been on Basie.
86.q: No, no. In fact, we didn't even know Basie had a small band. Freddie Green and I and the trombone player, Ted Donnelly, we met in front of the Theresa (Hotel) one afternoon and somebody -- somebody not even a musician -- said, man, how come you all are not going to Chicago? I said, "What do you…

86.t: Depression, not drinking, and no warning from Basie
86.s: Edison says he never drank, was afraid, was married, and recounts joining Basie around 21 in late 1937.
86.q: Yeah. I never did drink. Never had no desire for it, you know. And I was really -- I was afraid. I didn't know where I was going to get any money from and what I was going to do. I was really depressed.

86.t: Hurt by Basie's decision and why he went small
86.s: Edison says it really hurt and guesses Basie's swing style did not fit the modern trend.
86.q: Sure, anything. But we never expect those things to happen. Then when he told me he had gone without me, that really hurt me.

107.t: Old heads versus new material in the Basie band
107.s: He enjoyed the band but fought critics who wanted only old Basie, while Basie himself had been open to experiments.
107.ch: Leading the Basie band and recordings
107.q: And you’re not alone in that attestation. But as leader of the Basie Orchestra I enjoyed standing in front of a quality group every night and hearing this music coming back at me played so wonderfully, so beautifully. That was the best part of it, being on stage with all those great musicians. Some…

107.t: How Basie led: Marshall Royal and Freddie Green
107.s: With one finger Basie led an easy-going band, with Royal as straw boss and Green as sergeant at arms.
107.ch: Joining Basie and life on the road
107.q: We’ll start with Basie himself. One finger was all he needed to lead that band. He raised this finger and he might -- when he brought that finger down, music came from everywhere. As far as being a disciplinarian, he was very easy. He didn’t crack the whip. He wasn’t an a-h to get along with. He…

107.s: Taking over ended his other bands; he enjoyed top musicians but fought a feud with those wanting only old Basie.
107.ch: Current bands, plans and the second Basie tenure
107.q: I thought that you hadn’t asked me about the second Basie period from 1986 to 1995. Actually I thought we had covered parts of that period in previous interviews, but if we haven’t I’ll talk about that.

107.t: Old versus new Basie and the road manager dispute
107.s: Foster describes the 'war in Basieland', the road manager's resistance and his decision to leave.
107.ch: Current bands, plans and the second Basie tenure
107.q: Right, exactly, yeah, only they were magnified in the fact that I had the disadvantage of being out front, having to program the music, and I didn’t have the advantage of playing the piano. When Basie wanted to set a tempo, he’d doodle around on the piano until he found the tempo, so there was…

107.t: Basie's death and the band afterward
107.s: Foster felt it ended an era; Freddie Green and Tee Carson kept authenticity alive, and Nestico wrote.
107.ch: Current bands, plans and the second Basie tenure
107.q: I felt like it was the end of an era and that there was a big hole in the music industry as a result. The fact that the band carried on -- and his right arm was still there, Freddie Green. That gave it some validity that carried it, or some momentum that carried it past -­

107.t: Lessons from Basie carried into his own band
107.s: He learned to keep numbers short, pulled non-Basie charts for his own book, and regards Freddie Green's death as the end of authenticity.
107.ch: Current bands, plans and the second Basie tenure
107.q: With the Basie orchestra I had a bunch -- everybody in there was the cream. So I got accustomed to this quality, while being unaccustomed to this power struggle and all these things that were restricting me from being creative. That became a point of more and more frustration as time went on. But…

107.s: Foster and Hughes praise Sonny Payne, lead players and the rhythm section as the New Testament band.
107.ch: The late-1950s Basie band and closing
107.q: You know the thing with the juggling the sticks, throwing the sticks up and catching them and hitting right on a given beat, and this was, when you catch an audience with a visual extravaganza as well as a aural or musical—

107.s: Their contact was mostly about arrangements, and Foster called him Chief or Bas with deep respect.
107.ch: Arranging and style in the Basie band
107.q: Mostly when I had access to him on other levels, so to speak, we might be talking about an arrangement he wanted me to do.

107.t: Suppressing a second personality in Basie's band
107.s: Foster says his creative urges strained against demands for strictly Basie sound.
107.ch: Current bands, plans and the second Basie tenure
107.q: Yeah, I was suppressing a whole ’nother personality that was straining to get out. When people were saying, “We don’t want to hear this new stuff. We just want to hear the old Basie,” that was something -- I couldn’t accept that, because my creative urges were just bulging. They’re trying to get…

107.t: How Basie became leader after Bennie Moten
107.s: Hughes explains that after Moten died the band chose the easygoing Basie as front man.
107.ch: Basie band: origins, sound and style
107.q: Yeah, well, Basie was playing the piano in that band of course. And sometime down the line, Benny died. And the guys decided they wanted to get something going, and they formed a group, I think it was a small group at that point, but they decided that they wanted Basie to do the out front thing.…

68.t: Joining Basie: the trial in Kansas City and breakfast with Prez
68.s: Tate receives the telegram after Herschel Evans's death and meets Lester Young in the Kansas City hotel lobby.
68.q: Oh, no, in '39, when Herschel died, they knew me. I had a -- actually, I had a better chance than anybody. Ben tried to get the gig, Chu Now they in New York and they're names, you understand what I mean. And -- but they didn't, so I get a telegram from Basie to meet the band in Kansas City and…

68.t: Hearing the Basie band, its members and Jack Washington
68.s: Tate hears the band play a dance and discusses Freddie Green, Shad Collins and Jack Washington.
68.q: I'll tell you later on what happened in Philadelphia. So anyway, that night, I went down and listened to him play the colored dance and I went down and listened to that band. Boy, phew. And something says, "Well, maybe you better go on back to Nat Tole." You know, I says, "Shith --" (Laughter.)

68.t: Playing Blue and Sentimental to win the Basie job
68.s: The crowd calls for Herschel's feature and Basie asks Tate to play it; he rises to the occasion.
68.q: Yeah, yeah. Some of them didn't know and some of them -- you know how a crowd can get sometime. If one starts something, it'll continue. "Blue / Sentimental, and man, Blue / Sentimental." Basie says, "I can't." The featured artist is dead." And you hear some of them say, "Yeah, you know that. He's…

68.t: Basie as a leader: no cliques, shared hardships and the train car for families
68.s: Basie stays in the same lodging as the men and paid for a rail car so wives and children could travel.
68.ch: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
68.q: Then next week it would be you and Sweets, me and Basie -- Basie was just like all the cats. He really didn't act like a leader until -- but he got respect. He got respect and he still does. But he's just one of the guys. He's not the kind of leader that would go to a town and the band's staying…

68.s: Tate describes Basie's rule that you can do what you like but must play on the bandstand, and he introduces Paul Gonsalves.
68.ch: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
68.q: this: You can do anything you want to do. He doesn't get in your business and everything. But when you hit that band-stand, you got to play. Ain't no way in the world he would go through some things like Duke had gone through with some of his guys, no, not with Basie. He'd fire anybody if he comes…

68.t: Basie fires Paul Gonsalves in Detroit
68.s: Gonsalves misses a morning rehearsal in Detroit and Basie gives him two weeks' written notice.
68.ch: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
68.q: So Basie says 7:30 and if you go out and hang out with him just because you go out and hang out with him at a bar and get juiced and you go home and go to bed and don't make it, don't think that's going to save you, you know what I mean, because he's going to go there if he had to go sit on

68.t: Byas fired by pay envelope; Lester Young returns
68.s: Basie fires Byas, who does not remember the night, and Lester rejoins.
68.ch: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
68.q: So he carried him on up there. So the next day, Basie sent him his two weeks notice. And to show you how he is when he drinks, Henry knocked on the door -- Henry Snodgrass, the valet -- he says, "Yeah." He says, "Brought you something." It was in an envelope. He says, "Here it is."

68.t: Lester had recommended him; waiting on the bandstand
68.s: Basie remembers Tate from 1936; Tate sits at the back with his horn in its bag.
68.q: Prez was telling me -- oh, yeah, he was telling me they didn't fit. So he says, "There are a lot of other ladies that don't fit." He says, "But you've got the sound and everything is there. It'll be your engagement if you're playing like you were when I heard you last." So that night, what had…

68.s: He played in Basie's short-lived first band in Little Rock and rejoined after Moten died, in 1939.
68.q: Well I was with Basie’s first band in 1932 or 33, which was short-lived, and actually he was working with Benny Moten at that time. But Moten was having a lot of problems with getting work. So Basie got a job in I think it was Little Rock, Arkansas. And he came to Little Rock and I was there, and I…

388.t: Sitting in with Basie on brushes before Jo Jones
388.s: Basie, unhappy with his drummer, asks Leeman to sit in; he plays brushes while out of work with the stranded Murphy band.
388.q: Well, he and Lips were my friends, and when I'd go up -- and Basie eventually asked me to sit in, I was scared to death, but I played a little. He wasn't too happy with his drummer. I'll give you his name later on, I can't think of it now. It's not Jo Jones, though.

388.t: Returning to the Reno Club and hearing Jo Jones
388.s: Back after six months, Leeman hears the Basie band with Jo Jones, finds the music overwhelming and is told to play brushes on the next set.
388.q: No. Some of the people I did not know their names. The piano player, Jay McShann could tell you -- he knew everybody. I didn't get to know him that good, but he was forming bands in those days. I can't put my finger on them, though -- my memory isn't all that good.

388.t: Watching Basie build the band: Lester Young, Freddie Green, Walter Page
388.s: He was there the night Hammond and Goodman called, and saw Basie add Lester Young, a guitarist, Hershel Evans and Walter Page.
388.q: That's the Fall of '34 and the Spring of '35. I was there the night that John Hammond and Benny Goodman called from Chicago, and asked Basie if he wanted to leave and go to to the Grand Terrace -- I was there that night. I saw them flip; I was around there that Spring of '35, again, when they were…

388.t: The unhired regular drummer while Jo Jones came in late
388.s: Jo Jones arrived late each night so Leeman held the drum chair at the start of the evening, until he felt he could never play like Jo and Basie insisted he keep going.
388.q: Jo Jones, you asked me about -- Jo Jones always played at home with his family, he was very happy; he had children, or that was the story -- and he always used to come in an hour and a half to two hours late nights while I was in town, which was for two or three weeks, and he would depend upon…

388.t: Wanting to play Basie-style drums in Shaw's band
388.s: Leeman has Jo Jones and Basie in mind but Shaw wants something different, and nobody in the east knows the Kansas City band.
388.q: You see, drumnistically, I was forming in my mind the routines that we were playing, but I still had Jo Jones instilled in the back of my mind and the Basie band, and that's the kind of music I like, along with my records of Duke Ellington.

388.t: Arriving in Kansas City in spring 1934
388.s: After playing Denver, where they followed Bennie Moten's band, the Murphy band reaches Depression-era Kansas City, wide open with crime and jazz.
388.q: Gardens -- and we followed a band in there that was called Benny Moten's Orchestra. Now I remember following them in, and I only bring this up because Bennie Moten, shortly after that was operated on, I think, for a tonsil, and had died, and we hit Kansas City and Count Basie had taken a band into…

388.t: Boots Castle takes him to hear Basie at the Reno Club
388.s: A woman called Boots Castle guides him to the Reno Club on 12th Street, where he hears the Basie band with Lips Page, Buster Smith and Jimmy Rushing.
388.q: Well, I was walking down the street on a Sunday night, and I met a girl who asked me what I was looking for and I said, 'music'.

388.t: Joining Dan Murphy's Musical Skippers in 1933
388.s: A local bass player recommends him to territory bandleader Dan Murphy, whose naval-uniformed young band included Jimmy Blake and Ray Conniff.
388.q: Well, I was a little shy about approaching people. My eyes would open wide, but rather than -- which I should have done, but I didn't have that kind of a background. It happened a year or so later after I got out of my home town. After I got out of my home town, I went out in '33 -- Dan Murphy's…

388.t: Importance of recording the Kansas City years
388.s: Leeman and Jo Jones never talk about Kansas City because no one would understand; Hinton stresses the importance of the record and Leeman calls it a hot bed of jazz.
388.q: Well, Jo Jones -- if we were in a club or something, Jo just looks at me and if there are any other people around, he says, "Kansas City?" and he shakes his head, and I shake my head -- no sense in talking about it because nobody would know what we were talking about.

227.t: Basie and Lunceford as the real innovators
227.s: Mandel says Basie and Lunceford were the source of swing and the white bands pale imitations, though he praises Tommy Dorsey's Sy Oliver book with Buddy Rich.
227.q: Yeah, yeah, I loved that from the very beginning. When I stated hearing Basie and Lunceford I realized that’s where it was really all coming from, that these were the innovators, not the white bands I was hearing which were really pale imitations. And in the days I started hearing them, you know in…

227.t: What Basie's band meant to Mandel
227.s: Mandel says Basie had a profound effect on him; he loved all the Basie bands, even the early head-arrangement ones.
227.q: Profound. Profound, I liked that band better than any band I’ve ever liked. To this day I still liked – I liked the early sloppy bands, much better than I did the one that was reorganized that I was in. Although I loved that, that was the best experience I ever had playing with anyone, but we’ll…

227.s: Because Elliot Lawrence's band was not full-time, Mandel wrote for Basie and was called to join, replacing Jimmy Wilkins as second trombone.
227.ch: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
227.q: It was not a full-time working band, that's right, and therefore I started writing for Basie who had reorganized and was really sounding marvelous up at the Savoy and places like that and one day he called me to come in the band and that's when I was gone from Elliot. How could you turn something…

227.t: Meeting Basie as a cadet: it's the way we play it
227.s: Mandel recalls Earl Warren, Buddy Tate and Sweets taking him under their wing and Basie telling him it isn't the music but the way the band plays it.
227.ch: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
227.q: What a beautiful guy, but I had known him over the years you know, I’d be in bands and we’d come across each other. And I met him when I was a kid, when I was at the New York Military Academy, I used to come in and see the band at the Lincoln. And he said something to me then I remember, Earl…

227.t: Dates with Basie and the unrecorded charts
227.s: They fix Mandel's Basie stay as June to November 1953; his chart Straight Life was recorded and he laments how little of his work was.
227.ch: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
227.q: I got something that was recorded from – I’ve had very bad track record of getting things recorded by bands, I’ve also had a terrible record of getting soundtracks for all the movies I’ve done, recorded. I have very little recorded history laying around, why, I don't know maybe that's my karma.

227.t: What playing in Basie's band felt like
227.s: Mandel says Basie was the only band that felt inside as it sounded outside, praising the rhythm section and Basie's influence on Buddy Rich.
227.ch: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
227.q: Well, I never played in Woody's [Herman] band, that band that I thought was so wonderful, I'm sure it might have been a similar experience in the sense that, usually when you’d hear bands and you like the way they sounded, when you got inside and started playing with them it started falling apart…

227.t: Basie sax section, Neal Hefti and Ernie Wilkins
227.s: Mandel notes the Franks and Lockjaw joining, then praises arrangers Ernie Wilkins and Neal Hefti for easy-playing, swinging charts.
227.ch: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
227.q: Jaws [Eddie “Lockjaw” Davis] was in the band twice while I was there, Lockjaw. The two Franks came into the band while I was there, Frank Foster and Frank Wess, the band just kept getting better.

227.t: Quitting Basie and choosing writing over playing
227.s: Mandel regrets leaving Basie but says writing kept pulling him from playing, so at about 29 he stopped; Billy Byers and Bob Brookmeyer kept both.
227.ch: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
227.q: Well I had thought I had a way of getting into Warner Brothers, it turned out I didn't at all and then I was really kicking myself for having left Basie. I should never have done it, but you know I do those kind of things for 5 minutes and then go on to something else and forget about. And you know…

759.t: Basie as a boss and the young trumpeter he fired
759.s: Basie never told players what to play; Miles tells of a new trumpeter fired before playing a note for sassing him, and of the band as a unit.
759.q: Oh, he was wonderful, he was wonderful, he just — (if I’d known we were going to do this I would have brought a blue towel, I hope this is in color.) He was a wonderful boss because he never told you what to do or what to play. I asked our road manager, band manager at that time it was Sonny Cohn,…

759.s: Basie used eyebrow raises, head tilts and shoulder lifts to direct Butch, and never signalled displeasure.
759.q: No he didn’t, and that’s a good question too. Basie had a series of signals that he would give to me. Raising the eyebrows was one. Raising the eyebrows meant to increase the volume or to get ready for the explosion. That’s how — that’s how physical he would become on the bandstand. You know, we’re…

759.s: Freddie Green once stopped playing and shook his head at the new drummer; other Basie drummers got the same look.
759.q: Freddie Green, the great Freddie Green, you know, the great guitarist, Mr. Time we called him, was on the band all his life practically. And I was new on the band. I’d been on the band a few months. And I was playing, I was learning the charts and things were going pretty good. And one night, which…

759.t: Freddie Green as the band's metronome and Basie's tempos joke
759.s: Freddie's unamplified guitar set the tempo over Basie's, until Basie quietly hoped to play his own tempos while Green was in Florida.
759.q: Well that was divided between Freddie and Basie. And that leads to another story. Welcome to story time with Uncle Butch, children. Freddie was so strong in that band, no microphone. He wasn’t amplified in any way, but he was so strong. You could always hear him and always feel him when he was…

759.t: Growing up on the Basie bus
759.s: Butch says life on the Basie band matured him and that only Buddy Rich and Muhammad Ali could back up their boasts.
759.q: It is. You’re absolutely right about that. I learned so much, and I did so much growing up on that bus and those one-nighters, and those stages and gig after gig after gig and meeting people, myriads of different folks from all walks of life who either loved the music or hated the music. It was…

759.t: Replacing Ray Pirello and first night with the Basie band
759.s: He explains how he filled in for the injured new drummer, got the job, the three bass players named John, and joining with no rehearsal.
759.q: Well it’s an interesting story. A young man had been hired by Basie by the name of [sounds like] Ray Pirello. And he’d just been with the band a few weeks when he was in a very bad car accident in Chicago and wound up in the hospital. And Basic called me to come fill in, which I did. Originally I…

418.t: Best bands he worked in and the honour of being in Basie's band
418.s: He names Speed Webb and Thamon Hayes among the best bands and says he was honored to be in Basie's band.
418.ch: Early bands, Calloway to Basie and Kansas City (third typescript)
418.q: Yeah, I was very honored to be in that band. Yeah. And I did have a ball while I was in there. I was playing with some of the guys that were really great, you know. And there were -- lots of greatness dead or alive you know. Like prayers, you know.

418.t: Few rehearsals in Basie's band, drinking and being fired
418.s: In his time the Basie band rehearsed once or twice a week; he drank, dozed under the stage lights, got few solos in the crowded stage shows and was fired.
418.ch: Early bands, Calloway to Basie and Kansas City (third typescript)
418.q: Well there was, because when I was in the band we didn't do all that much rehearsing you know. We didn't do all that much rehearsing. We rehearsed maybe once or twice a week. You understand? And it was the guy in the music and then later got. And probably that's when left the band you know. I got…

418.t: Best bands he worked in and the honour of being in Basie's band
418.s: He names Speed Webb and Thamon Hayes among the best bands and says he was honored to be in Basie's band.
418.ch: Small groups, Europe and Kansas City memories (repeated passages)
418.q: The Thamon Hayes band. That was a good band. Let's see... Well, most all those bands I played with were good bands, you know.

You understand? It was a different brand of music than what they later got. And probably that's when Prez left the band,…

418.s: He names Speed Webb and Thamon Hayes among the best bands and says he was honored to be in Basie's band.

237.t: Count Basie playing blues on the Eblon organ
237.s: After Scott, Basie joined as organist and played blues during a tense silent-film scene; Lovett scolded him and he behaved.
237.q: Well, Basie never played -- he hadn't been on organ very long, you understand what I mean? You know, organs are very loud instruments which everybody knows you put one finger on there and run everybody out of town. So they had one of those pictures where a guy was slipping up on a woman, you…

237.t: Basie's telegram and joining his band in 1942
237.s: Basie's booker wired him to join in New Jersey; he filled in for the ill Jo Jones for about six weeks without rehearsal.
237.q: Yes. Jo -- when he sent for me, Jo were ill at the time, you know, and he sent for me.

237.t: Benny Moten's start in houses and Lyric Hall, the BB&D trio
237.s: Goodwin recalls Benny as a youth playing piano in brothels, then leading a trio at Lyric Hall about 1922.
237.ch: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
237.q: Benny wasn't much more than a kid himself and he was playing in these -- well, these houses of ill-repute, these whorehouses and so forth, and he was doing this by himself. Well he did this -- well he was -- actually I don't think Benny was of age when he was doing this but he was such an…

237.t: Basie arrives in Kansas City and takes the piano at the Bluebird
237.s: Goodwin says Basie came about 1927 stranded with Gonzelle White's show and surprised Dude Knox's band at the Bluebird.
237.ch: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
237.q: They played here at the Gayiety Theatre and they became stranded -- they ran out of money. I guess the money that they made at the Gayiety didn't help them too much because they broke up here.

237.t: Basie as sideman; Lee's and Moten's the two top bands
237.s: Basie scrambled for gigs but wanted Moten's band; Goodwin says Lee and Moten led the town and Lovett joined Lee about 1927-28.
237.ch: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
237.q: It was in the '20s I know.

237.t: How Basie talked his way into Moten's band for Wichita
237.s: Basie sat in for Moten, then showed up packed at the record shop and went to Wichita on a cut of others' pay.
237.ch: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
237.q: Oh, this is a story. Basie had a -- well first of all, Baby had a -- Benny had a -- he used Basie off and on, you know. Basie liked the band so well he would hang around and he didn't want any money. He just wanted the pleasure of playing with Benny.

103.t: One night with Basie in Topeka; Lester Young's chorus on "After You've Gone"
103.s: Walter Page invites him to join Basie; after one night in Topeka, shaken by Lester Young's solo, he refuses pay and decides to return to school.
103.q: Joined them in Joplin. The job went out; I came into Kansas City and I played piano and I had my vibraphones. I wasn't going to play drums and I only played any two jobs in six weeks. I was playing a special dance, Tommy Douglas's band was playing, and Walter Page came up and sat in the band and he…

103.t: Staying two weeks that became fourteen years with Basie
103.s: Returning for his drums, he is talked into staying; he told Basie he'd play two weeks until a drummer was found, and it lasted 14 years.
103.q: I didn't join them. I come back to pick up my drums with Jimmy Jewell that - where you played all the dances at the Dreamland Ballroom and they told me, you can't leave. Ben Webster and

103.t: Recording "The King" in 1946 and the band's postwar personnel
103.s: Jones tells how he showed the band a groove on a sock cymbal for "The King," with Emmett Berry's solo and J. J. Johnson's last date.
103.ch: Return to Basie and leaving in 1948
103.q: Which he says, his is mine. I didn't know it was mine till after, because they had been recording for about 3 hours and I walked in with a sock cymbal and I said, 'Shadow, get up for a minute. Let me have this band for a minute. Fellows, it goes like this.' That's the last recording that J. J.…

103.t: Walter Page, Joe Keyes and Ben Webster try to keep him in the band
103.s: Page, Ben Webster and Joe Keyes pressure him to join Basie, but he insists he can only play five or six pieces.
103.q: Walter asked me to go to play with him. Of course Mac Washinton was going to play with Benny at the Harlem Club on 15th-La Salle. Ben Webster, Walter Page, and Joe Keyes had me -

103.t: Walter Page's Blue Devils, Rushing and Basie moving to Moten
103.s: He describes Walter Page's Blue Devils, how Jimmy Rushing left first, then Basie, joining Bennie Moten.
103.q: Well, I'll tell you what had happened. Walter Page had the greatest band that I ever heard in my life. Now remember, I was running around, Milt. I used to go to Detroit and what have you when they had Edwards

103.t: Fletcher Henderson's band in Kansas City, December 1933
103.s: He recalls Fletcher Henderson's band visiting with Coleman Hawkins, Bobby Stark and Dickie Wells, and going around with Stark.
103.q: 1933, because December 18th, 1933, I will never forget Fletcher Henderson's band coming to Kansas City and Herschel Evans and Lester Young with Ben Webster at the Cherry Blossoms Ballroom, when Coleman Hawkins got drunk and Dickie Wells was right there and laughed at him.

98.t: Basie's band at the Grand Terrace and Chicago versus Kansas City
98.s: Basie and Jo Jones came to Chicago from Kansas City without show experience; Saunders compares Chicago's show demands with Kansas City's jazz players.
98.q: So a band playing in one of those places, they had to be very, very versatile. And -- I keep getting back to Basie, and -- like I told you about this thing, about Basie and this Willie Berg. Anyway, I was talking about him and he was telling me about when they were in the Grand Terrace, had just…

98.t: How his friendship with Basie developed in Chicago
98.s: Basie's band left the Grand Terrace in slow winters, came to the DeLisa breakfast shows, and Saunders got close to Jo Jones.
98.ch: Pianists, Basie, Lil Armstrong and closing
98.q: Yeah, well, see, I had met him in Kansas City before that. And they had a habit at the Grand Terrace when business was bad, like, this winter, we had -- Fox would sent everybody home. But Mike DeLisa, he never did, he kept his doors open regardless is it was one person in there or two or 100.

98.s: Basie took his trumpeter Sonny Cohn, and Saunders was upset until Basie offered arrangements.
98.ch: Pianists, Basie, Lil Armstrong and closing
98.q: Well, after that it was periodic. And then the thing about it, he would steal my men, and I'd get mad as hell, yeah. And when he took Sonny Cohn, that was the thing. That was my first trumpet player. I almost died. But then he'd say, that's all right, I'll send you some arrangements.

98.t: Planning the fiftieth anniversary guests: Basie band and Louie Bellson
98.s: Basie's band will play, Sonny Cohn is arranging it, and he hopes Louie Bellson will come.
98.ch: Pianists, Basie, Lil Armstrong and closing
98.q: Yeah, he's going to be at the 50th anniversary, and no problem of getting him at all. He was only too happy. I talked with Sonny, the musical director. He takes care of most all of the business.

98.t: Bennie Moten's band, Thamon Hayes, Ben Webster and the start of Basie's band
98.s: The summer job at Fairmount Park moved from Moten to Thamon Hayes, Ben Webster came to town, Lester Young played with George Lee, and Basie's band emerged from Moten's after the Cherry Blossom opened.
98.q: Right, right, right, right, yeah, see, so Piney and -- he was living there, and Jesse Stone was living there, Vic. Dickenson had just come. They had -- when I was there, I was there for about six months, and during this six months was the time when Benny Morton's band and Thamon Hayes -- see, Benny…

98.t: Moten's band, battles of bands and the riff behind One O'Clock Jump
98.s: Moten's band played the Harlem against Ellington and built riffs on tunes like Moten's Swing; Saunders and DeMichael discuss where Basie's One O'Clock Jump riff came from.
98.q: Pardon me. So that was -- that was the way these sessions -- and then, they had a battle of bands in there. See, Benny Moten's band would play at the Harlem and they would have Duke Ellington's band. And then it was one of those things where -- you know, and Benny and them --

220.t: Studying flute on the GI Bill and Basie's calls to join
220.s: Wess earned a flute degree while Basie kept calling for a tenor player; Basie promised more exposure and let him play flute solos.
220.q: was looking for a tenor player you know, so he kept calling and calling. He called for a couple of years and I told him I was doing something, you know, and I couldn’t leave right then. So he just kept calling. Periodically he would call. And in the meantime I got a degree, a bachelor’s degree in…

220.t: Over eleven years with Basie, joining with Milt Hinton
220.s: Wess spent over eleven years with Basie and joined the same day as Milt Hinton.
220.q: Yeah. Milt Hinton and I joined the band the same day.

220.t: Playing the world with Basie and recommending musicians
220.s: The band was one of Basie's best; Wess recommended many players such as Eddie Jones, Thad Jones, Sonny Cohn and Al Aarons.
220.q: Oh, we always had a good following. And the band was hot. We were in one of the best bands Basie ever had. And that’s the band that made him rich, you know. The band was tight. I had forgotten actually, how good the band was until I was listening to those Mosaic recordings. And then it came back to…

220.s: Wess, playing third alto, told Basie to hire Eric Dixon as tenor.
220.q: Yeah, I told him to call Eric because you know I was playing third alto, and he put me there because he knew I could play first if Marshall wasn’t there, you know, he always kept somebody in the third chair that could play lead, so that he would never be without a lead player, you know. So he kept…

220.t: Who gets the solos in the Basie band
220.s: Solo assignments are up to the bandleader.
220.q: Yeah. He says you take this and you take that. It’s up to him, you know.

115.t: Sitting in with Basie's band at the Cherry Blossom
115.s: Jo Jones lets him play one number with Basie's band, with Eddie Durham and Walter Page in the rhythm section.
115.ch: Kansas City, Omaha and Lloyd Hunter
115.q: Yeah, they were playing at the Cherry Blossom. And I went by to hear the band. And Jo said, "Come on, sit in and play with the band." And everybody gave me a dirty look when I sat down. I played one number and got off of that stand.

115.t: First stint with Basie, replacing Jo Jones and Shadow Wilson
115.s: Jo Jones recommended Gus; he joined Basie in late 1947, finished the Strand Theatre, then was displaced when Shadow Wilson returned.
115.q: The first time I got with Basie, I stayed with him until -- and we went in the Strand Theatre. Now, that's -- I took Jo Jones' place after he took Shadow's place. And so he left and told them to get me to work with Basie.

115.t: Personnel of the new Basie big band
115.s: He recalls Jaws, Frank Foster, Frank Wess, Charlie Fowlkes, Marshall Royal, the Wilkins brothers and bassist Eddie Jones.
115.q: not when we first started. He picked up Frank and West later. I think Frank Foster was in there first, then Frank West, and he had Charlie Fowlkes.

115.t: Back in the Basie studio after the hospital; Sonny Payne
115.s: After leaving hospital he sat in on a Basie date, and Basie kept the flashier Sonny Payne.
115.q: Sonny Payne. And they made a record date and I went down and made a session. And not that day but about, I'd say, about a month later I made a session with Basie because something happened. Sonny didn't show up, and I don't know what happened, but he wasn't there. And they was out looking for a…

115.t: The small band without Freddie Green
115.s: The first small-band job at the Brass Rail lacked Freddie Green, Gus insisted he be rehired, and Clark Terry shone.
115.q: Oh, yes, Freddie was out of the band. I said, 'Where's Freddie Green?' He said, 'Well, I got this job in Chicago and I booked just for a small band, six pieces.' I said, 'Man, you better get Freddie Green back in this band,' just like that. And we made the job in Chicago, at the Brass Rail. And…

105.t: Basie band after Prez, and Buddy Tate
105.s: He argues nobody filled Prez's chair in Basie's band, with Rowe naming Buddy Tate.
105.q: Exactly. It’s not putting Fred or Buddy down or putting anybody down, it’s just that I’m a different person. And my newest, the “Timely” album, is living proof of hey, you might not like it as well but hey what the hell, it’s what I’m doing now. Somebody likes it because it’s been moving. And I’m…

105.t: Back in LA in 1945, the Floyd Ray band, and Jo Jones puts the sticks in his hand
105.s: After the army he found bebop in LA, enrolled at the Conservatory, played with Floyd Ray's band, and Jo Jones brought him to the Lincoln Theater to take his place with Basie.
105.q: And I’ve always been -- I’ve been very fortunate, man. I’ve always worked. I’ve never had really -- I always got a gig. As a matter of fact, man, when I was --more or less put it like this. After I came out of the service, I went back to LA. In the meantime I go back to LA and this is 1945, and the…

105.t: Filling in with Basie without music
105.s: He played the Basie show from memory, learned from Sweets to follow the lead trumpet part, toured the coast for a couple of months and read Jimmy Mundy's new charts.
105.q: Yeah. Anyway we come back and we have a rehearsal at the Club Alabam and Jimmy Mundy brings in some new charts, right. Man, I read those things like they was going out -- a lot of the cats in the band were scuffling and everything. Man, I just -- things like Queer Street, you know, all those -- I…

105.t: Basie's rhythm section and meeting Jo Jones at the Dunbar Hotel
105.s: Basie's sound turned him around from Lunceford's two-beat; Jo Jones became his hero and Lee Young took him to meet Jo at the Dunbar Hotel when he was 14 or 15.

935.s: At twelve, Don Lamond got Duffy up to play Shiny Stockings with Basie; years later in Florida he played again when Sonny Payne was unwell.

935.s: Touring strain and Basie's reluctance to rest after Japan 1980, birthday parties, the Kennedy Center Honors Whirly Bird solo for Ella, and Joe Williams's kiss telling him to relax.

811.t: Joining Basie: names for the Chief, Sammy Davis and the first night
811.s: Basie hires him personally; he plays with Sammy Davis at Harrah's, meets Freddie Green's stare and plays Wind Machine in Toledo.
811.q: Yeah the guys called him a various assortment of names. Bill, Chief. I called him Chief. Some guys called him Count. Other guys called him Boss. 936.t: Writing to the Basie band and learning its book

145.t: How Basie and Ellington let people go; Basie's luck

145.t: Basie's hiring through recommendations; his heart attack

145.t: Section leader and rehearsal master of the Basie band

70.t: Basie's band the most consistent he played with

566.t: Dicky Wells, 'Fat Fanny' and the Basie band as a happy family

566.s: Dance relays stories that Basie let a sick Charlie Fowlkes go while he was in hospital. Humes had never heard it and doubts Basie would have done it himself.

473.s: John had told them about Basie's Kansas City band before it came east; when it opened at Roseland, Stuff's group went over and played a couple of numbers as greeters.
473.q: See, when we come in, Basie hadn't come to town yet, because John was coming in the place and he was telling us about this great band out in Kansas City, you know, that he'd heard.

239.t: Basie band discipline on the Birdland bus tour
239.s: The Basie band sounded fresh after long bus rides near Butte, Montana, and Jones considers how Basie and Ellington hold bands together.
239.ch: Sarah Vaughan and the Basie band
239.q: And I've been -- I've experienced that thing, especially with the Basie band. I think the other day I was speaking about when we were doing one nighters on the bus, and we'd gotten near Butte, Montana someplace. This was the Birdland show. And the guys had sat up so long, their feet began to swell.…
